methodology: The study employed ring-opening polymerization (ROP) for the synthesis of cyclic propylene oxalate polymers. The reaction was conducted under controlled conditions including temperature and catalyst presence. Polymerization without catalyst was also investigated to understand its effect on the final product.
research_objective: To investigate the polymerization of six-membered cyclic propylene oxalate, focusing on understanding the role of catalysts in the process, as well as exploring the impact of polymerization conditions and additives.

key_findings.finding: Ring-opening polymerization (ROP) was observed for cyclic propylene oxalate, with high limiting conversion of about 96% at 100 °C in the presence of tin(II) octoate.
Polymer cross-linking reaction occurred during ROP, resulting in partial (about 30%) conversion of the catalyst into insoluble tin(II) oxalate.
Polymerization without catalyst was significantly slower (2000 times), leading to formation of polymer with Ð ~ 2, indicating a first-order kinetics process.
Synthesis of POx via polycondensation by heating diols with oxalic acid under reduced pressure yields hazardous ethylene glycol.
ROP of cyclic propylene oxalate in the presence of Sn(Oct)2 forms linear polymers with hydroxyl groups at the chain ends and about 10% of cyclic oligomers.
Polymerization of cyclic oxalates can be controlled by the addition of benzyl alcohol as an initiator.
Cyclic oxalate polymerization is a challenging but promising area for designing biodegradable polymers.
